doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

title: The near future of jazz
summary: Thomas recalls his 1985 radio show, the lack of a shared language, and urges musicians to know fundamentals.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well, to wrap up here, what’s your feeling about the near future of jazz?

Hmm. The near future of jazz. That’s a good question. You know when I was here I had a radio show on WHCL and my very last show, the very last two songs I played, I said well what’s the future of jazz going to be like. This was like ’85 you know, spring of ’85. And I said some people say it’s going to be like this, and I played Jean-Luc Ponty with his guitar doing something that was very fusionesque. And I said but I kind of would like it to be like this — and I put on Art Blakey with Wynton Marsalis. Swinging you know. So I think that jazz has flowered in such a fashion that, as Branford Marsalis once said to me, there isn’t these days the shared language, the lingua franca, as there was at one time, so that you have these different strains, these different offshoots where there are some people who are so much into complex time signatures, you know, nine, eleven, and seven-eight and all kinds of stuff, as opposed to or — not just as opposed to — but where straight four-four swing, maybe it’s boring to them or something. But I would add that to the voice of the blues, voice of swing, and this need, the seeming need to go into all these complexities. But as Clark Terry, in that great documentary Keep On Keeping On said to a group of students at William Paterson University and Duke Ellington said once something along the lines that simplicity is one of the most complex things that you can
Yeah. It’s not easy to be simple.

So but to answer your question, it’s kind of hard to say. I can tell you what I wish. I want to make sure that as people experiment, as musicians try in their definition of their own style maybe in relation to a group of musicians that they play with even a generation, that they will continue to look at the sweep and continuum of the history of development, know it, know how to play aspects of that so they can always draw on that as they’re trying to innovate or do something else. But I mean there’s such a diversity that you find. So if you want this mixture, I mean there’s folks from a South or East Indian background that incorporate Indian music into what they do. There are people from Eastern Europe who incorporate their own sound. And they should. They should. Because that’s part of their own expression, their own background. But I would say, like with anything in life, you have your fundamentals and then you develop based on your fundamentals. Know your fundamentals if you’re going to play in the art form of jazz, know the fundamentals and certain aspects of the fundamentals, blues, jazz, four-four swing, Latin — you can add that Latin tinge — you know there’s a certain thing. You can play at a variety of tempos, from ballad to up-up tempo; learn how to play in before you play out. If you want to play out, to be able to play out then that’s counterposing what in is. So learn in first you know. Get your basics down and then go from there.
